paragraphs: Friend, here's the big idea. The writer spent twenty verses in the dark, and then he says, "Yet I call this to mind, and therefore I have hope:" (Lamentations 3:21). His hope doesn't come from a better situation. It comes from what he remembers about the LORD: "His mercies never fail. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!" (Lamentations 3:22-23).

So what do we do while the hard stuff is still happening? The writer says, "The LORD is good to those who wait for Him, to the soul who seeks Him" (Lamentations 3:25). Waiting here isn't pretending the pain isn't there. He says even if the Lord causes grief, "He will show compassion according to His abundant loving devotion" (Lamentations 3:32), and the Lord "will not cast us off forever" (Lamentations 3:31). I think that's the part to hold onto when the hard stretch feels like it will never end.

Here's what that means for you, baker. You can be honest about the hurt AND still say, "The LORD is my portion" (Lamentations 3:24). The writer also says the Lord "does not willingly afflict or grieve the sons of men" (Lamentations 3:33), and that Lord is the One in charge of both adversity and good (Lamentations 3:38). So when tomorrow morning shows up, look for His mercy there. I'd bet it's already waiting on the counter, fresh out of the oven.
